findings.issue_text: [BUG] Provider selection becomes nondeterministic for providers with equal order() values because Comparator.comparingInt(...).reversed() is stable and falls back to ServiceLoader classpath ordering. DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider (and FIPS1402Provider) all return order() == 200, so a deployment with default and elytron (or fips) providers on the classpath gets whichever the ServiceLoader happens to find first — which varies with jar ordering — and the previous hard failure that protected against ambiguity is now only a debug-level log, so a server can silently start with the wrong crypto provider (e.g. non-FIPS when FIPS was required).

[BUG] concatenatedRSToASN1DER builds two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances whose output is discarded before constructing the real signature, so the executed path performs redundant allocation and the code misleads readers into thinking those writes matter. No functional break (the final encoder re-writes r and s), but the dead writes are wasted work on every ECDSA signature verification and any future edit that assumes the earlier encoders contribute output will produce wrong DER; the dead statements should be deleted.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the JRE default keystore provider (e.g. SUN/SunJSSE), not a BouncyCastle Provider, violating the interface contract the method name promises. Any caller in the authz-client path that passes the returned Provider to Signature.getInstance/KeyFactory.getInstance expecting BC will get a provider that lacks BC algorithms and throw NoSuchAlgorithmException; the Keycloak server's DefaultCryptoProvider semantics are silently diverged for library consumers.

[ADVISORY] Adding a non-default order() method to the CryptoProvider interface breaks binary compatibility for out-of-tree implementations, which still lack the method after this diff. Custom/third-party CryptoProvider jars compiled against the old interface load fine via ServiceLoader but throw AbstractMethodError at the new Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order) call site inside CryptoIntegration.detectProvider, turning a working deployment into a hard startup failure after upgrade.

[ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init is only invoked in create(Configuration), so AuthzClient instances built via `new AuthzClient(configuration)` or the other create overloads that bypass this method never initialize the crypto provider. Any code path constructing AuthzClient directly (tests, embedding code that already holds a Configuration) hits CryptoIntegration.getProvider() with an uninitialized classloader and either fails with the 'Not able to load any cryptoProvider' IllegalStateException or picks up the wrong classloader's provider.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs and discards two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) before building the real output, so these lines are dead code. A maintainer refactoring the ECDSA conversion will read these writes as producing part of the result and mis-edit the method; the dead calls also allocate on every signature conversion in the JWT-verification hot path.

[ADVISORY] The test only asserts round-trip equality asn1derToConcatenatedRS → concatenatedRSToASN1DER → asn1derToConcatenatedRS, so any symmetric error (e.g. swapping the R and S halves in both conversion directions, or off-by-one in the split) passes the test. A regression that produces structurally valid but semantically wrong R||S output (which breaks ECDSA signature verification in consumers) ships green; the test never verifies the converted signature against a known-good value, e.g. by using it in `Signature.verify`.

[ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS has a malformed-input branch (`seq.size() != 2` → IOException) that no test in the diff exercises, and the ASN1Decoder's error paths (truncated DER, high-tag-number rejection, out-of-bounds length, negative DER integers passed through integerToBytes) are entirely uncovered. The diff adds a hand-rolled ASN.1 parser whose whole purpose is to reject malicious/corrupt signatures, and none of its rejection paths are verified; a regression in readLength or readTagNumber would silently accept malformed tokens during JWT verification, and the next refactor of this file will have no safety net.

[ADVISORY] detectProvider now resolves multiple providers by order, but DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so a tie between the server-side providers is broken by unspecified ServiceLoader ordering. Any deployment that ends up with two of the three order-200 providers on one classpath gets a nondeterministically chosen provider (FIPS vs non-FIPS) depending on classpath enumeration order — a silent, environment-dependent security-relevant behavior change from the old hard failure; the order() mechanism as shipped does not actually order the providers it was written to order.

[BUG] CryptoIntegration.init is called only inside create(Configuration), so any code path that obtains an AuthzClient without passing through that factory (e.g. `new AuthzClient(configuration)` via the public constructor, or whatever create(InputStream) delegates through) never initializes the crypto provider and later token-verification code fails with IllegalStateException("Not able to load any cryptoProvider...") from CryptoIntegration.getProvider(). Library consumers building the client through the constructor directly get a runtime failure at first EC-signature use instead of at creation time, and there is no test in the diff covering an un-init'd getProvider() call path.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK's default KeyStore provider (`KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`), which is not Bouncy Castle and typically not the provider any caller of a method named getBouncyCastleProvider expects. If any code path reaches this method expecting BC-specific classes (e.g. BC-only KeyStore formats or BC-provider-backed operations), it receives the Sun provider and fails at runtime; the diff adds no verification of which entry points into CryptoProvider the authz-client actually exercises, so the suitability of this stub is unverified.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs two ASN1Encoder instances whose output is discarded before building the real sequence, leaving dead work on the hot path. Any caller converting a concatenated ECDSA signature to DER pays two wasted ByteArrayOutputStream allocations per signature (per token signature verification on the authz client), and the next editor reading the method must determine whether the first two write calls are load-bearing before changing the encoding — the dead statements fail the deletion test (deleting them changes nothing functionally).

[BUG] detectProvider deletes the fail-fast IllegalStateException for multiple crypto providers on the classpath and instead silently logs-and-ignores all but the highest-order provider, a cross-cutting change to server-side boot behavior that is not traceable to the PR's stated intent of adding an authz-client crypto provider. A Keycloak server operator who accidentally ends up with two crypto providers on the classpath (e.g., default plus FIPS jars) previously got a hard error at startup identifying the conflict; now the server silently boots with whichever provider ServiceLoader + order ranking happens to pick, so a misconfigured FIPS deployment can run with the non-FIPS provider and violate its compliance requirement with no warning above debug level. The only justification is the authz client's own jar now shipping a provider, which is handled by order(); the previous invariant protected every other deployment and is dropped without a requirement asking for it.

[ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init is wired only into the static create() factories while the public AuthzClient(Configuration) constructor remains a supported path that performs no crypto initialization, so the provider registration the diff exists to deliver is not enforced as an invariant of the class. A user (or in-tree caller such as tests or wrapping SDKs) constructing AuthzClient via the constructor or deserializing from a Configuration directly gets ECDSA signature handling that fails or falls back to an unregistered provider, and the failure surfaces far from the construction site. The init belongs in the constructor (or a lazy guard) so every instance path — not just the two factory methods — guarantees the provider is loaded.

[ADVISORY] The order() mechanism (order added to CryptoProvider, three existing providers set to 200, sorting added to CryptoIntegration) is cross-cutting infrastructure shared across the whole server, but the only consumer of the ranking is the authz-client jar conflict scenario, so the design couples a server-wide selection policy to a single client's packaging need. Any future provider (or a downstream product fork adding its own CryptoProvider) now inherits an undocumented tie-breaking policy where equal order() values (all three existing providers return 200) resolve by ServiceLoader iteration order, which is classpath-order dependent and non-deterministic across environments — the next contributor adding a provider will get silently deprioritized or prioritized behavior they cannot reason about without reading this diff. The stated intent only required that the authz-client jar not break the server; a narrower fix (exclusion or namespacing) would not have introduced a global precedence field.

[BUG] Removing the multiple-provider error and replacing it with order-based selection makes ties (all three existing providers return order 200) resolve by arbitrary ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. A FIPS deployment that accidentally has both crypto/fips1402 and crypto/default (or crypto/elytron) jars on the classpath previously failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'; now DefaultCryptoProvider can be silently selected over FIPS1402Provider (or vice versa) depending on jar classpath order, so a FIPS-mode server runs with the non-FIPS provider with no error or log line above DEBUG level.

[BUG] The authz-client jar globally registers AuthzClientCryptoProvider as a CryptoProvider service, so embedding authz-client on any classpath with keycloak-common silently installs a stub provider whose getAlgorithmProvider, getSignature, getPemUtils, etc. all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Any application that adds keycloak-authz-client for the authorization API and also uses other keycloak-common functionality (PEM parsing, cert utils, AES ciphers, signature instances) crashes with UnsupportedOperationException at runtime when no higher-order provider is present; conversely, in the Keycloak server itself the authz-client jar now participates in crypto-provider selection, a boundary the authz client module previously did not cross.

[BUG] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default KeyStore provider (typically SUN) instead of a BouncyCastle provider, violating the CryptoProvider contract every existing implementation honors. Any keycloak-common code path that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() to obtain or register BC (the documented purpose of the method) silently receives the wrong provider in a standalone authz-client deployment, producing algorithm-not-found or wrong-provider failures instead of a clear error.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs two discarded ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and same for s) immediately before building the real DER sequence, dead code. The next editor reading this method assumes all four encoder calls contribute to the output; a maintenance change to the dead pair has no effect on the signature, masking intent and inviting a wasted fix or accidental removal of the live lines.

[ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init is now called on every AuthzClient.create() invocation, coupling client-instance creation to a JVM-global static initialization of the crypto SPI. Every create() re-runs ServiceLoader discovery; if an application already initialized CryptoIntegration with a different classloader (e.g., an app-server deployment), creating an AuthzClient re-detects providers against the authz-client's classloader, potentially swapping the active global CryptoProvider out from under other keycloak-common users in the same JVM.

[BUG] detectProvider silently replaces the previous fail-fast IllegalStateException on multiple crypto providers with silent selection of the highest-order provider, changing an accepted safety invariant of the server without any human-accepted requirement. A Keycloak server deployment with both the FIPS and default providers on the classpath used to abort startup with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' — an operator in a FIPS-mandated environment now gets a silently non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider (order tie at 200 resolved by arbitrary ServiceLoader classpath order) and processes secrets under non-validated crypto with no error.

[BUG] DefaultCryptoProvider.order() returns 200, identical to FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider, so the 'higher order wins' selection rule cannot actually discriminate between the server crypto providers and falls back to arbitrary ServiceLoader ordering on the tie. When default and fips1402 (or elytron) jars coexist on the server classpath, which crypto provider the server runs with is decided by classpath jar order, not by any declared preference — the stated intent of the order field ('higher number has preference') is unfulfilled for exactly the multi-provider cases the field was added to resolve.

[ADVISORY] AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements most CryptoProvider methods with UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet') and registers itself via META-INF/services with order 100, so it only ever wins selection when it is the sole provider — meaning the new ordering mechanism added to CryptoIntegration exists to make this half-implemented provider coexist with server providers rather than to express a real preference. Any authz-client embedding where another CryptoProvider is visible to the AuthzClient classloader silently bypasses this provider entirely, and any caller that does reach it via a path requiring getAlgorithmProvider, getPemUtils, getSignature, etc. (e.g. token verification or TLS truststore wrapping in embedded use) hits a runtime UnsupportedOperationException with no compile-time or startup signal — a hidden coupling between the provider's partial coverage and whichever code paths the AuthzClient actually exercises.

[ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) on every invocation, changing the provider-detection contract for embedders from 'provider detected once by whoever initializes' to 're-detected whenever a client is created'. An application that embeds authz-client on a classpath where it also initialized a server CryptoProvider now gets the AuthzClientCryptoProvider SPI file loaded during provider re-detection; if the authz-client jar's services entry is visible to that classloader, a create() call can re-select the client provider over the previously accepted one, flipping the active CryptoProvider for already-running code mid-process.

[ADVISORY] The change removes the fail-fast on multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath and silently selects the highest-order one, converting a detectable misconfiguration into a silent provider downgrade. An operator who accidentally ends up with both a FIPS and a non-FIPS crypto provider on the classpath (e.g., by adding authz-client, which now ships its own META-INF/services CryptoProvider at order 100, into a server deployment) gets no error and runs with whichever provider wins the order comparison; in a FIPS-compliance-required deployment the previously-loud IllegalStateException that caught this now only emits a debug-level log line nobody reads, so a non-compliant crypto stack ships silently. Tie orders (DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider both return 200) make the winner dependent on ServiceLoader iteration order, which is JVM/jar-order dependent.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JCA default KeyStore provider rather than a BouncyCastle (or equivalent) Provider, so any caller using it to obtain BC-specific algorithms (as the CryptoProvider contract implies) silently falls back to whatever the JVM default is. Client code that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC capabilities (e.g., for PEM parsing or BC-specific algorithm names) gets the SUN/default provider and fails at runtime with NoSuchAlgorithm/PemUtils errors only when the specific operation is attempted, and the provider's own getPemUtils/getCertificateUtils/getX509CertFactory all throw UnsupportedOperationException, so token/JWKS operations needing them crash deep inside AuthzClient usage rather than at init where the cause would be diagnosable.

[ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS accepts DER integers of arbitrary size/sign and integerToBytes silently truncates (keeps only the low qLength bytes) when the decoded r or s exceeds the expected coordinate length, and also accepts negative integers, instead of rejecting malformed signatures. Signature bytes coming from an untrusted JWT are mangled rather than rejected during the concatenated-RS conversion used in ES256/384/512 verification: a signature with an oversized or negative r/s is converted to a wrong-but-well-formed value and fails verification with a confusing non-security error (or, for values whose truncated form collides, relies entirely on the downstream verifier for rejection), where the Keycloak DefaultCryptoProvider equivalents validate lengths; anyone debugging token verification against a hostile issuer gets garbage-in behavior instead of a clean 'invalid signature encoding' rejection.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (two single-integer encoders whose output is discarded) before building the real sequence, indicating copy-paste leftover dead computation in the security-critical signature path. No behavioral defect (the final writeDerSeq re-encodes rBigInteger/sBigInteger correctly), but the dead lines confuse future maintainers of a signature-serialization routine into editing the wrong encoder chain, increasing the risk that a subsequent change alters signature encoding; deletion test: removing lines 93-94 removes two statements with zero output effect.

[ADVISORY] The ECDSA tests are mirror round-trip tests that never verify the converted signatures against a consumer of the format, so an encoding that is self-consistent but not spec-valid DER passes all three tests. If concatenatedRSToASN1DER emitted a non-interoperable encoding (wrong tag octet, missing minimal-encoding rule, wrong INTEGER padding), the round trip asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) would still return x and testES256/384/512 stay green; the first victim is any JWS verifier (server-side token validation) receiving an authz-client-produced ES256 signature that fails verification. Checked: the only test-shaped file in the diff is this one, and its sole assertion (line 58 assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)) is the round-trip identity — it never asserts the ASN.1 output equals a known-good DER encoding, nor that Signature.initVerify on the ASN.1 form verifies.

[ADVISORY] detectProvider's behavioral contract changed from 'throw IllegalStateException on multiple providers' to 'pick highest-order provider and log the rest', with zero test modifications in the diff. The previous guarantee that misconfigured classpaths fail fast is now silently replaced by order-based selection; a deployer with both FIPS and default providers on the classpath who previously got a hard error now silently gets whichever has the higher order() — a FIPS compliance regression nobody notices because no test asserts the selection or logging behavior. Checked all test-shaped files in the diff (authz/client/src/test/.../ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java only): no test references CryptoIntegration, detectProvider, or order().

[ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create now invokes CryptoIntegration.init as an unconditional side effect, but the diff contains no test that create() triggers provider detection or that it fails safely when no provider is on the classpath. A consumer calling AuthzClient.create (the library's main entry point) now hits ServiceLoader scanning; if authz-client is dropped on a classpath where CryptoProvider services are absent or duplicated, create() throws IllegalStateException where previous releases constructed the client fine — an untested behavior change in the public API. Checked ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java: it instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly and never touches AuthzClient or CryptoIntegration.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs two dead ASN1Encoder instances (lines 103-104 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);') whose output is discarded, and the tests exercise the method without ever failing on this dead code. The round-trip test passes whether or not these dead writes exist, demonstrating the test exercises the code path but not its correctness of construction; the dead statements mislead the next maintainer into thinking they contribute to the output, and a refactor 'cleaning them up' or worse 'wiring them in' would pass the same green tests.

[ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS's new edge-case branches — non-2-element sequences, integerToBytes' truncation and left-padding paths, and the ASN1Decoder error paths (EOF, negative length, high tag numbers) — have no test that triggers any of them. A regression in integerToBytes trimming (e.g., an off-by-one that drops the sign byte of an r value whose top bit is set) silently produces invalid signatures only for the ~50% of ECDSA signatures where r or s has its high bit set or leading zeros; the diff's tests use one keyPair and one signature per curve (generated in the constructor, line 43), so the padding branches can go either way by chance per run, making failures flaky-undetected rather than reliably caught.

[ADVISORY] The test class generates its KeyPair in the constructor and reuses a single KeyPair/curve across ES256, ES384 and ES512 tests, so the three tests do not actually exercise the curve-specific signature lengths with matching curves. KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") defaults to a single curve (typically secp256r1, giving 64-byte r||s); signing with ES384/ES512 Java algorithms on a P-256 key either throws or produces 64-byte signatures fed into asn1derToConcatenatedRS with signLength 96/132 — the test then verifies padding/truncation of the wrong-size data rather than real 384/512-bit signatures, so the ES384 and ES512 assertions do not verify the behavior they claim (real-world P-384/P-521 signature conversion).

[BUG] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM's default KeyStore provider (typically SUN), not a BouncyCastle provider, despite the method contract and name. Any caller that requests getBouncyCastleProvider() to obtain BC-specific algorithms (e.g., BC PEM handling, BC keystore formats) silently gets the default JDK provider and fails at runtime with NoSuchAlgorithmException or missing-function errors that name the wrong provider during debugging.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs and discards two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) whose output is never used. Dead code that misleads the next maintainer into thinking those encoders contribute to the returned signature; the real encoding happens in the following writeDerSeq block, and a future edit touching the dead lines risks diverging from the live ones.

[BUG] readInteger() passes readLength()'s -1 return (indefinite-length encoding) straight into read(length), which executes `new byte[-1]` and throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException. A malformed/indefinite-length DER signature handed to asn1derToConcatenatedRS escapes the declared `throws IOException` contract with a raw NegativeArraySizeException instead of an IOException, breaking any caller that catches IOException to handle bad input.

[ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init() is added to only one create() overload (the hunk header shows it inside create(InputStream configStream)), leaving the public AuthzClient.create(Configuration) path without provider initialization. Embedders (e.g., policy enforcer or tests) that build an AuthzClient directly from a Configuration object get IllegalStateException('Not able to load any cryptoProvider') the first time ECDSA signature conversion runs, even though the same configuration works via the InputStream overload.

[ADVISORY] Provider selection now sorts only by order(), but WildFlyElytronProvider and DefaultCryptoProvider both return order() == 200, so ties fall back to ServiceLoader classpath order. An application with both elytron and default crypto jars on the classpath silently gets whichever provider the classloader enumerates first, with only a debug-level 'Ignored crypto providers' log — the deterministic-failure contract of the old explicit IllegalStateException is replaced by environment-dependent behavior.

[ADVISORY] Most CryptoProvider methods (getAlgorithmProvider, getPemUtils, getCertificateUtils, getX509CertFactory, getSignature, getKeyPairGen, createECParams, etc.) throw UnsupportedOperationException while the provider is registered as the highest-availability service for the authz-client classloader. Any authz-client code path that grows to touch one of these methods (e.g., PEM parsing of a realm public key during token validation) crashes with a raw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime instead of a meaningful error about the missing capability.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added test `authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java`, the assertion is only `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)` after doing `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign) -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rsConcat) -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS(asn1Des)`. This round-trip property can still pass if both conversion methods share the same symmetric mistake (e.g., swapping R/S or consistent mis-splitting), because the test never checks the semantic correctness of the conversion (e.g., by verifying a signature using the converted form or comparing against an independent/known-good encoding).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS has a malformed-input branch (`seq.size() != 2` → IOException) that no test in the diff exercises, and the ASN1Decoder's error paths (truncated DER, high-tag-number rejection, out-of-bounds length, negative DER integers passed through integerToBytes) are entirely uncovered. The diff adds a hand-rolled ASN.1 parser whose whole purpose is to reject malicious/corrupt signatures, and none of its rejection paths are verified; a regression in readLength or readTagNumber would silently accept malformed tokens during JWT verification, and the next refactor of this file will have no safety net.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces nontrivial, security-relevant parsing/validation logic in the new hand-rolled ASN.1 code (e.g., `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS` throws on `seq.size() != 2`; `ASN1Decoder` has multiple rejection/error paths in `readTagNumber`/`readLength`/`read`). The only added test (`ECDSAAlgorithmTest`) exercises only the happy-path roundtrip on valid signatures and does not cover any malformed-input/rejection branches. This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in test coverage rather than a directly verifiable functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] detectProvider now resolves multiple providers by order, but DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so a tie between the server-side providers is broken by unspecified ServiceLoader ordering. Any deployment that ends up with two of the three order-200 providers on one classpath gets a nondeterministically chosen provider (FIPS vs non-FIPS) depending on classpath enumeration order — a silent, environment-dependent security-relevant behavior change from the old hard failure; the order() mechanism as shipped does not actually order the providers it was written to order.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` to `sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` and no longer throws when `foundProviders.size() > 1`; it just returns `foundProviders.get(0)` and logs the rest as "Ignored". In the same diff, `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all implement `order()` returning `200`, so the sort does not deterministically select among them when more than one is present. With equal `order()`, the chosen provider depends on the `ServiceLoader.load(...)` iteration order, which is not specified, making provider selection environment-dependent and silently different from the previous hard-failure behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] CryptoIntegration.init is called only inside create(Configuration), so any code path that obtains an AuthzClient without passing through that factory (e.g. `new AuthzClient(configuration)` via the public constructor, or whatever create(InputStream) delegates through) never initializes the crypto provider and later token-verification code fails with IllegalStateException("Not able to load any cryptoProvider...") from CryptoIntegration.getProvider(). Library consumers building the client through the constructor directly get a runtime failure at first EC-signature use instead of at creation time, and there is no test in the diff covering an un-init'd getProvider() call path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff only shows `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` being added to `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)`, but it does not show (a) that `AuthzClient` has a public constructor usable by consumers, nor (b) that any other public factory/entry point (e.g., `create(InputStream)`) bypasses `create(Configuration)` and thus skips init. The claimed runtime failure path and missing test for an un-initialized `CryptoIntegration.getProvider()` call are not directly verifiable from the provided diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK's default KeyStore provider (`KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`), which is not Bouncy Castle and typically not the provider any caller of a method named getBouncyCastleProvider expects. If any code path reaches this method expecting BC-specific classes (e.g. BC-only KeyStore formats or BC-provider-backed operations), it receives the Sun provider and fails at runtime; the diff adds no verification of which entry points into CryptoProvider the authz-client actually exercises, so the suitability of this stub is unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` with `getBouncyCastleProvider()` implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is typically the JDK provider (e.g., SUN) and not Bouncy Castle. This is a concrete, diff-grounded mismatch with what callers would reasonably expect from a method named `getBouncyCastleProvider` (and from the broader Keycloak crypto provider design). However, within this diff there is no demonstrated code path in authz-client that actually calls `getBouncyCastleProvider()` (the new test only exercises ECDSA signature format conversion via `getEcdsaCryptoProvider()`), so an actual runtime failure is plausible but not verifiable from the patch alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs two ASN1Encoder instances whose output is discarded before building the real sequence, leaving dead work on the hot path. Any caller converting a concatenated ECDSA signature to DER pays two wasted ByteArrayOutputStream allocations per signature (per token signature verification on the authz client), and the next editor reading the method must determine whether the first two write calls are load-bearing before changing the encoding — the dead statements fail the deletion test (deleting them changes nothing functionally).

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, there are two standalone statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose returned encoders are not stored or used. The actual returned value is built by a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger))...`. Therefore those two earlier calls perform dead work (extra ASN1Encoder/ByteArrayOutputStream allocations and integer encoding) without affecting output, which is a concrete performance/maintainability issue but not a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] detectProvider deletes the fail-fast IllegalStateException for multiple crypto providers on the classpath and instead silently logs-and-ignores all but the highest-order provider, a cross-cutting change to server-side boot behavior that is not traceable to the PR's stated intent of adding an authz-client crypto provider. A Keycloak server operator who accidentally ends up with two crypto providers on the classpath (e.g., default plus FIPS jars) previously got a hard error at startup identifying the conflict; now the server silently boots with whichever provider ServiceLoader + order ranking happens to pick, so a misconfigured FIPS deployment can run with the non-FIPS provider and violate its compliance requirement with no warning above debug level. The only justification is the authz client's own jar now shipping a provider, which is handled by order(); the previous invariant protected every other deployment and is dropped without a requirement asking for it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` explicitly removes the previous fail-fast `IllegalStateException` when `foundProviders.size() > 1` and instead sorts providers by the new `CryptoProvider::order` (descending) and returns the first one, only logging the rest at `debug` level. This is a verifiable, cross-cutting behavioral change in server boot/provider selection policy (silent preference over hard error) introduced alongside adding an authz-client crypto provider and the new `order()` API, but it’s not inherently a correctness bug given the new ordering mechanism appears intentional.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init is wired only into the static create() factories while the public AuthzClient(Configuration) constructor remains a supported path that performs no crypto initialization, so the provider registration the diff exists to deliver is not enforced as an invariant of the class. A user (or in-tree caller such as tests or wrapping SDKs) constructing AuthzClient via the constructor or deserializing from a Configuration directly gets ECDSA signature handling that fails or falls back to an unregistered provider, and the failure surfaces far from the construction site. The init belongs in the constructor (or a lazy guard) so every instance path — not just the two factory methods — guarantees the provider is loaded.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader());` added only in the static factory `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` (AuthzClient.java), and there is no corresponding change shown to the `AuthzClient` constructor path (still invoked via `new AuthzClient(configuration)`). If callers can instantiate `AuthzClient` directly (constructor use is not shown in the diff), they would bypass the new crypto integration initialization that this PR appears to rely on (new `CryptoProvider` SPI entry under `META-INF/services` plus ECDSA conversion logic). This is a design/robustness concern grounded in the diff, but the diff alone does not prove the constructor is public/supported or that missing init definitively breaks runtime behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The order() mechanism (order added to CryptoProvider, three existing providers set to 200, sorting added to CryptoIntegration) is cross-cutting infrastructure shared across the whole server, but the only consumer of the ranking is the authz-client jar conflict scenario, so the design couples a server-wide selection policy to a single client's packaging need. Any future provider (or a downstream product fork adding its own CryptoProvider) now inherits an undocumented tie-breaking policy where equal order() values (all three existing providers return 200) resolve by ServiceLoader iteration order, which is classpath-order dependent and non-deterministic across environments — the next contributor adding a provider will get silently deprioritized or prioritized behavior they cannot reason about without reading this diff. The stated intent only required that the authz-client jar not break the server; a narrower fix (exclusion or namespacing) would not have introduced a global precedence field.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a global precedence mechanism to shared infrastructure: `CryptoProvider` now requires `int order()` and `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(...)` sorts `ServiceLoader` results by descending order and picks the first (`.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`). All existing server providers return the same value `200` (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider), while the new authz-client provider returns `100`, implying the change is primarily to avoid the authz-client provider winning when co-located. With equal `order()` values, selection falls back to `ServiceLoader` iteration order (encounter order), which is classpath-dependent and not explicitly documented in code, making future provider interactions hard to reason about. This is a cross-cutting design/architecture concern rather than a directly verifiable functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Removing the multiple-provider error and replacing it with order-based selection makes ties (all three existing providers return order 200) resolve by arbitrary ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. A FIPS deployment that accidentally has both crypto/fips1402 and crypto/default (or crypto/elytron) jars on the classpath previously failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'; now DefaultCryptoProvider can be silently selected over FIPS1402Provider (or vice versa) depending on jar classpath order, so a FIPS-mode server runs with the non-FIPS provider with no error or log line above DEBUG level.

adjudication.rationale: In `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider`, the previous fail-fast on `foundProviders.size() > 1` was removed and replaced with sorting by `CryptoProvider::order` and selecting `foundProviders.get(0)`, only logging ignored providers at DEBUG. In this diff, `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all return the same `order()` value (200), so ties are not broken deterministically and will depend on `ServiceLoader` iteration/classpath order. This makes it possible for an unintended provider (e.g., non-FIPS) to be silently chosen when multiple are present, with no warning/error above DEBUG, which is a real behavioral/security regression introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The authz-client jar globally registers AuthzClientCryptoProvider as a CryptoProvider service, so embedding authz-client on any classpath with keycloak-common silently installs a stub provider whose getAlgorithmProvider, getSignature, getPemUtils, etc. all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Any application that adds keycloak-authz-client for the authorization API and also uses other keycloak-common functionality (PEM parsing, cert utils, AES ciphers, signature instances) crashes with UnsupportedOperationException at runtime when no higher-order provider is present; conversely, in the Keycloak server itself the authz-client jar now participates in crypto-provider selection, a boundary the authz client module previously did not cross.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a global ServiceLoader registration for `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` in authz-client (`authz/client/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/...`) pointing to `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`. That provider implements `CryptoProvider` but most methods (`getAlgorithmProvider`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getPemUtils`, `getSignature`, `getAes*Cipher`, etc.) throw `UnsupportedOperationException` (see `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java`). `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, which triggers provider detection via ServiceLoader. While `CryptoIntegration` now prefers higher `order()` (authz-client sets `order()` to 100, others set 200), if an application has `keycloak-common` + `keycloak-authz-client` on the classpath without another crypto provider module, the only discovered provider will be this stub and it will be selected, causing runtime failures when any unsupported crypto functionality is used. The change to `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` also stops throwing on multiple providers and instead silently picks the highest-order one, so authz-client indeed participates in selection whenever present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default KeyStore provider (typically SUN) instead of a BouncyCastle provider, violating the CryptoProvider contract every existing implementation honors. Any keycloak-common code path that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() to obtain or register BC (the documented purpose of the method) silently receives the wrong provider in a standalone authz-client deployment, producing algorithm-not-found or wrong-provider failures instead of a clear error.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()` (see `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java`), which returns the provider for the JVM default KeyStore type (typically a SUN provider), not a BouncyCastle provider. This contradicts the `CryptoProvider` interface method intent (`getBouncyCastleProvider()`), and differs from existing implementations (e.g., `DefaultCryptoProvider` / `FIPS1402Provider` returning BC/BCFIPS). In an authz-client-only classpath (where this is the only `CryptoProvider` via the added `META-INF/services/...` file), `CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider()` will therefore return a non-BC provider, which can lead to wrong-provider/algorithm issues as described.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs two discarded ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and same for s) immediately before building the real DER sequence, dead code. The next editor reading this method assumes all four encoder calls contribute to the output; a maintenance change to the dead pair has no effect on the signature, masking intent and inviting a wasted fix or accidental removal of the live lines.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` each create a new encoder, write into it, and then discard it without using the resulting bytes. The actual returned DER output is built by a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger))...`. This is diff-verifiable dead code that can mislead maintainers, but it does not change runtime behavior (the returned value is unaffected), so it’s not a correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init is now called on every AuthzClient.create() invocation, coupling client-instance creation to a JVM-global static initialization of the crypto SPI. Every create() re-runs ServiceLoader discovery; if an application already initialized CryptoIntegration with a different classloader (e.g., an app-server deployment), creating an AuthzClient re-detects providers against the authz-client's classloader, potentially swapping the active global CryptoProvider out from under other keycloak-common users in the same JVM.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now unconditionally calling `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, which ties per-client construction to a JVM-global crypto SPI initialization and forces the init path to run with the authz-client’s classloader each time. The diff also changes provider detection to select the highest `CryptoProvider.order()` rather than failing on multiples, making the chosen global provider depend on what `ServiceLoader.load(..., classLoader)` returns for that classloader. While the diff doesn’t show `CryptoIntegration.init(...)` internals (so it’s not provable that it will always re-detect and overwrite an existing global provider), the new call site + classloader-dependent selection is a concrete architecture/scope concern introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] detectProvider silently replaces the previous fail-fast IllegalStateException on multiple crypto providers with silent selection of the highest-order provider, changing an accepted safety invariant of the server without any human-accepted requirement. A Keycloak server deployment with both the FIPS and default providers on the classpath used to abort startup with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' — an operator in a FIPS-mandated environment now gets a silently non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider (order tie at 200 resolved by arbitrary ServiceLoader classpath order) and processes secrets under non-validated crypto with no error.

adjudication.rationale: In common/CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(), the previous fail-fast behavior on multiple CryptoProvider implementations (throwing IllegalStateException when foundProviders.size() > 1) is removed. The new code sorts by CryptoProvider::order descending and returns foundProviders.get(0), only logging the rest at DEBUG. In this diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all implement order() returning 200, so when multiple are present the selection is not deterministic (tie-breaking depends on ServiceLoader iteration/classpath order). This can lead to silently choosing an unintended provider instead of aborting, which is a real correctness/security risk introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] DefaultCryptoProvider.order() returns 200, identical to FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider, so the 'higher order wins' selection rule cannot actually discriminate between the server crypto providers and falls back to arbitrary ServiceLoader ordering on the tie. When default and fips1402 (or elytron) jars coexist on the server classpath, which crypto provider the server runs with is decided by classpath jar order, not by any declared preference — the stated intent of the order field ('higher number has preference') is unfulfilled for exactly the multi-provider cases the field was added to resolve.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CryptoProvider.order()` with the documented intent that “higher number has preference”. `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` now sorts providers by `order` descending and returns `foundProviders.get(0)`. However, the three server-side providers shown in the diff (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`) all implement `order()` returning `200`, so the sort cannot discriminate among them. In that tie case, the chosen provider is simply whichever `ServiceLoader` yields first (encounter order), so the declared preference mechanism is effectively unfulfilled in the multi-provider scenario.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements most CryptoProvider methods with UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet') and registers itself via META-INF/services with order 100, so it only ever wins selection when it is the sole provider — meaning the new ordering mechanism added to CryptoIntegration exists to make this half-implemented provider coexist with server providers rather than to express a real preference. Any authz-client embedding where another CryptoProvider is visible to the AuthzClient classloader silently bypasses this provider entirely, and any caller that does reach it via a path requiring getAlgorithmProvider, getPemUtils, getSignature, etc. (e.g. token verification or TLS truststore wrapping in embedded use) hits a runtime UnsupportedOperationException with no compile-time or startup signal — a hidden coupling between the provider's partial coverage and whichever code paths the AuthzClient actually exercises.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered via META-INF/services and implements CryptoProvider, but most methods throw UnsupportedOperationException (e.g., getAlgorithmProvider/getPemUtils/getSignature/wrapFactoryForTruststore). It also returns order() = 100, while existing providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return 200, and CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() was changed to sort by order descending and no longer fails when multiple providers are present (it picks the first and logs others as ignored). Therefore, in any classloader where another CryptoProvider is visible, this new authz-client provider will be silently bypassed; and if it is selected as the only provider, unimplemented methods could cause runtime UnsupportedOperationException if exercised. Whether those code paths are actually hit by AuthzClient can’t be verified from the diff, so it’s more an architectural/robustness concern than a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) on every invocation, changing the provider-detection contract for embedders from 'provider detected once by whoever initializes' to 're-detected whenever a client is created'. An application that embeds authz-client on a classpath where it also initialized a server CryptoProvider now gets the AuthzClientCryptoProvider SPI file loaded during provider re-detection; if the authz-client jar's services entry is visible to that classloader, a create() call can re-select the client provider over the previously accepted one, flipping the active CryptoProvider for already-running code mid-process.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now unconditionally calling `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` before constructing the client. It also shows `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(...)` no longer failing when multiple `CryptoProvider`s are visible; it now sorts by `CryptoProvider::order` (new method) and silently chooses the highest-order provider, logging the rest as ignored. That is a real, diff-grounded architectural/contract change (global crypto selection may now be triggered from client creation, and multi-provider classpaths no longer hard-fail). However, the finding’s claim that init will “re-detect whenever a client is created” and “flip the active CryptoProvider mid-process” is not fully verifiable from this diff because `CryptoIntegration.init(...)` implementation/caching behavior is not shown here, and the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` has `order() == 100` while the built-in providers in the diff are set to `200`, making it unlikely to be re-selected over them in the default setup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The change removes the fail-fast on multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath and silently selects the highest-order one, converting a detectable misconfiguration into a silent provider downgrade. An operator who accidentally ends up with both a FIPS and a non-FIPS crypto provider on the classpath (e.g., by adding authz-client, which now ships its own META-INF/services CryptoProvider at order 100, into a server deployment) gets no error and runs with whichever provider wins the order comparison; in a FIPS-compliance-required deployment the previously-loud IllegalStateException that caught this now only emits a debug-level log line nobody reads, so a non-compliant crypto stack ships silently. Tie orders (DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider both return 200) make the winner dependent on ServiceLoader iteration order, which is JVM/jar-order dependent.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to no longer throw when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are present; it now sorts by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first, only logging “Ignored crypto providers” at debug (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). This makes provider selection potentially silent and, with ties, nondeterministic: DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so the chosen provider can depend on ServiceLoader encounter order/jar ordering. Additionally, authz-client now ships a service provider (META-INF/services/...CryptoProvider) at order 100, increasing the likelihood of multiple providers on the classpath. These behaviors are directly shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JCA default KeyStore provider rather than a BouncyCastle (or equivalent) Provider, so any caller using it to obtain BC-specific algorithms (as the CryptoProvider contract implies) silently falls back to whatever the JVM default is. Client code that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC capabilities (e.g., for PEM parsing or BC-specific algorithm names) gets the SUN/default provider and fails at runtime with NoSuchAlgorithm/PemUtils errors only when the specific operation is attempted, and the provider's own getPemUtils/getCertificateUtils/getX509CertFactory all throw UnsupportedOperationException, so token/JWKS operations needing them crash deep inside AuthzClient usage rather than at init where the cause would be diagnosable.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which will typically return the JVM’s default KeyStore provider (e.g., SUN) rather than BouncyCastle or an equivalent provider (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java`). This is a concrete mismatch with the `CryptoProvider` contract name/intent and could mislead any caller that uses this method expecting BC capabilities. Separately, the provider leaves `getPemUtils()`, `getCertificateUtils()`, `getX509CertFactory()`, etc. throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`, which means any code path that relies on those will fail at runtime, but the diff alone doesn’t show such a call path from `AuthzClient` beyond `CryptoIntegration.init(...)`, so the “will fail in AuthzClient usage” part isn’t directly verifiable here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS accepts DER integers of arbitrary size/sign and integerToBytes silently truncates (keeps only the low qLength bytes) when the decoded r or s exceeds the expected coordinate length, and also accepts negative integers, instead of rejecting malformed signatures. Signature bytes coming from an untrusted JWT are mangled rather than rejected during the concatenated-RS conversion used in ES256/384/512 verification: a signature with an oversized or negative r/s is converted to a wrong-but-well-formed value and fails verification with a confusing non-security error (or, for values whose truncated form collides, relies entirely on the downstream verifier for rejection), where the Keycloak DefaultCryptoProvider equivalents validate lengths; anyone debugging token verification against a hostile issuer gets garbage-in behavior instead of a clean 'invalid signature encoding' rejection.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider#asn1derToConcatenatedRS, DER INTEGERs are decoded via new BigInteger(bytes) (signed) and then converted with integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength). integerToBytes explicitly truncates when qLength < bytes.length by copying only the low-order qLength bytes, and it never rejects negative BigIntegers. Therefore oversized or negative r/s values are silently mangled into fixed-size coordinates instead of being rejected as malformed signature encoding, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (two single-integer encoders whose output is discarded) before building the real sequence, indicating copy-paste leftover dead computation in the security-critical signature path. No behavioral defect (the final writeDerSeq re-encodes rBigInteger/sBigInteger correctly), but the dead lines confuse future maintainers of a signature-serialization routine into editing the wrong encoder chain, increasing the risk that a subsequent change alters signature encoding; deletion test: removing lines 93-94 removes two statements with zero output effect.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, there are two standalone statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose results are not stored or used. The returned value is produced by a separate encoder chain that re-encodes r/s inside `writeDerSeq(...)`, so these two statements are dead/throwaway work and can confuse maintainers in a security-sensitive encoding routine. This is directly visible in the diff and is not a functional defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The ECDSA tests are mirror round-trip tests that never verify the converted signatures against a consumer of the format, so an encoding that is self-consistent but not spec-valid DER passes all three tests. If concatenatedRSToASN1DER emitted a non-interoperable encoding (wrong tag octet, missing minimal-encoding rule, wrong INTEGER padding), the round trip asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) would still return x and testES256/384/512 stay green; the first victim is any JWS verifier (server-side token validation) receiving an authz-client-produced ES256 signature that fails verification. Checked: the only test-shaped file in the diff is this one, and its sole assertion (line 58 assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)) is the round-trip identity — it never asserts the ASN.1 output equals a known-good DER encoding, nor that Signature.initVerify on the ASN.1 form verifies.

adjudication.rationale: The newly added test `authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java` only checks a round-trip identity: it converts a real JCA DER signature to concatenated RS, back to DER via `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER`, then back again and asserts `rsConcat == rsConcat2`. This is verifiable from the diff (the sole assertion is `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)`). The test never verifies that the DER produced by `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` is accepted by an independent consumer (e.g., `Signature.initVerify`), nor matches known-good DER constraints (minimal INTEGER encoding, correct tags/length). So it is a concrete, diff-grounded concern about test adequacy for the new ASN.1 encoding/decoding logic, but it does not prove an actual defect in the encoding itself from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] detectProvider's behavioral contract changed from 'throw IllegalStateException on multiple providers' to 'pick highest-order provider and log the rest', with zero test modifications in the diff. The previous guarantee that misconfigured classpaths fail fast is now silently replaced by order-based selection; a deployer with both FIPS and default providers on the classpath who previously got a hard error now silently gets whichever has the higher order() — a FIPS compliance regression nobody notices because no test asserts the selection or logging behavior. Checked all test-shaped files in the diff (authz/client/src/test/.../ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java only): no test references CryptoIntegration, detectProvider, or order().

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a concrete behavioral change in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider`: it now sorts loaded `CryptoProvider`s by `order()` descending and returns the first one, instead of throwing when `foundProviders.size() > 1` (the exception block was removed and replaced with debug logging of ignored providers). The new `CryptoProvider.order()` method and implementations (e.g., default/elytron/fips returning 200, authz-client returning 100) confirm the order-based selection is real. The diff also only adds an `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` unrelated to `CryptoIntegration`/`detectProvider`/`order()`, so there is no test coverage of this new selection behavior or the “ignored providers” logging path. This is a specific, diff-grounded review concern about changed misconfiguration handling and lack of tests, not a directly verifiable defect on its own.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create now invokes CryptoIntegration.init as an unconditional side effect, but the diff contains no test that create() triggers provider detection or that it fails safely when no provider is on the classpath. A consumer calling AuthzClient.create (the library's main entry point) now hits ServiceLoader scanning; if authz-client is dropped on a classpath where CryptoProvider services are absent or duplicated, create() throws IllegalStateException where previous releases constructed the client fine — an untested behavior change in the public API. Checked ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java: it instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly and never touches AuthzClient or CryptoIntegration.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows a new unconditional side effect in the public entry point: `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`. `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(...)` still throws `IllegalStateException` if `ServiceLoader` finds no `CryptoProvider` implementations, and the added `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` doesn’t exercise `AuthzClient.create` or `CryptoIntegration` at all (it instantiates `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` directly). However, the finding’s claim about duplicated providers causing an exception is not supported by the diff: `CryptoIntegration` was changed to sort by `order()` and no longer throws when multiple providers are present; it just logs ignored ones. The core concern (untested behavior change / init-triggered provider detection on create) is still specific and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs two dead ASN1Encoder instances (lines 103-104 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);') whose output is discarded, and the tests exercise the method without ever failing on this dead code. The round-trip test passes whether or not these dead writes exist, demonstrating the test exercises the code path but not its correctness of construction; the dead statements mislead the next maintainer into thinking they contribute to the output, and a refactor 'cleaning them up' or worse 'wiring them in' would pass the same green tests.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` each create a new ASN1Encoder, write to its internal buffer, and then discard it without using the result. The returned value is built from a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger))`, so the two earlier writes are dead code. The added round-trip test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) would still pass if those dead statements were removed, so it doesn't validate anything about them. This is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/test-quality issue, but not a functional defect in the produced output.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS's new edge-case branches — non-2-element sequences, integerToBytes' truncation and left-padding paths, and the ASN1Decoder error paths (EOF, negative length, high tag numbers) — have no test that triggers any of them. A regression in integerToBytes trimming (e.g., an off-by-one that drops the sign byte of an r value whose top bit is set) silently produces invalid signatures only for the ~50% of ECDSA signatures where r or s has its high bit set or leading zeros; the diff's tests use one keyPair and one signature per curve (generated in the constructor, line 43), so the padding branches can go either way by chance per run, making failures flaky-undetected rather than reliably caught.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces nontrivial ASN.1/ECDSA conversion logic with multiple new branches and error paths (e.g., `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`: `if (seq.size() != 2) throw...`; `integerToBytes` has both truncation and left-padding branches; `ASN1Decoder` throws on EOF, invalid high tag numbers, out-of-bounds/negative lengths). The only added test (`ECDSAAlgorithmTest`) performs a single sign/roundtrip per curve using one generated `KeyPair` and one signature, which does not deterministically exercise those branches and may or may not hit the padding/truncation cases depending on the random signature values. So the finding about missing targeted tests for these new edge cases is grounded in the diff; it’s a test coverage/robustness concern rather than a demonstrated functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test class generates its KeyPair in the constructor and reuses a single KeyPair/curve across ES256, ES384 and ES512 tests, so the three tests do not actually exercise the curve-specific signature lengths with matching curves. KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") defaults to a single curve (typically secp256r1, giving 64-byte r||s); signing with ES384/ES512 Java algorithms on a P-256 key either throws or produces 64-byte signatures fed into asn1derToConcatenatedRS with signLength 96/132 — the test then verifies padding/truncation of the wrong-size data rather than real 384/512-bit signatures, so the ES384 and ES512 assertions do not verify the behavior they claim (real-world P-384/P-521 signature conversion).

adjudication.rationale: In `ECDSAAlgorithmTest`, a single `KeyPair` is generated once in the constructor via `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` with no curve parameters, so it will use the provider default curve for all tests. The `test(ECDSAAlgorithm algorithm)` method then signs using the algorithm-specific `Signature` instance but always with that same key. For ES384/ES512, `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign, algorithm.getSignatureLength())` uses larger `signLength` (and thus `qLength`) than the key’s actual curve size; `integerToBytes(...)` will left-pad/truncate to fit, meaning ES384/ES512 tests can pass by padding P-256-sized r/s values rather than validating real P-384/P-521 signatures. This is a real, diff-grounded test validity issue rather than a production defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM's default KeyStore provider (typically SUN), not a BouncyCastle provider, despite the method contract and name. Any caller that requests getBouncyCastleProvider() to obtain BC-specific algorithms (e.g., BC PEM handling, BC keystore formats) silently gets the default JDK provider and fails at runtime with NoSuchAlgorithmException or missing-function errors that name the wrong provider during debugging.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()` (i.e., the provider of the JVM’s default KeyStore type), which is typically the JDK/SUN provider rather than BouncyCastle. This contradicts the method name/contract (`CryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider`) and can cause runtime failures or misleading provider selection if any caller expects BC-specific algorithms from this returned `Provider`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs and discards two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) whose output is never used. Dead code that misleads the next maintainer into thinking those encoders contribute to the returned signature; the real encoding happens in the following writeDerSeq block, and a future edit touching the dead lines risks diverging from the live ones.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` instantiate encoders, write values, and then discard them without using their output. The returned signature is produced only by the subsequent `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)).toByteArray();`. This is real dead code and can mislead maintainers, but it does not change runtime behavior (no defect) beyond minor overhead/confusion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] readInteger() passes readLength()'s -1 return (indefinite-length encoding) straight into read(length), which executes `new byte[-1]` and throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException. A malformed/indefinite-length DER signature handed to asn1derToConcatenatedRS escapes the declared `throws IOException` contract with a raw NegativeArraySizeException instead of an IOException, breaking any caller that catches IOException to handle bad input.

adjudication.rationale: In `ASN1Decoder.readInteger()`, the result of `readLength()` is used directly as the argument to `read(length)`. `readLength()` explicitly returns `-1` for indefinite-length encoding (`if (length == 0x80) { return -1; }`). Passing `-1` into `read(int length)` will execute `new byte[length]` with `length = -1`, which throws `NegativeArraySizeException` (unchecked) rather than the declared `IOException`. This can be triggered by malformed ASN.1/DER input flowing into `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(...)`, breaking callers that expect bad input to surface as `IOException`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init() is added to only one create() overload (the hunk header shows it inside create(InputStream configStream)), leaving the public AuthzClient.create(Configuration) path without provider initialization. Embedders (e.g., policy enforcer or tests) that build an AuthzClient directly from a Configuration object get IllegalStateException('Not able to load any cryptoProvider') the first time ECDSA signature conversion runs, even though the same configuration works via the InputStream overload.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader());` added inside `public static AuthzClient create(Configuration configuration)` (AuthzClient.java). The finding claims it was only added to the InputStream overload and that the Configuration path lacks initialization, but the shown change explicitly initializes in the Configuration overload, contradicting the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Provider selection now sorts only by order(), but WildFlyElytronProvider and DefaultCryptoProvider both return order() == 200, so ties fall back to ServiceLoader classpath order. An application with both elytron and default crypto jars on the classpath silently gets whichever provider the classloader enumerates first, with only a debug-level 'Ignored crypto providers' log — the deterministic-failure contract of the old explicit IllegalStateException is replaced by environment-dependent behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() to sort providers by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and to no longer throw when multiple providers are found; it selects the first and only logs ignored providers at debug (common/src/main/java/.../CryptoIntegration.java). In this diff, DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider both implement order() returning 200 (crypto/default/... and crypto/elytron/...), so ties are not deterministically broken by the comparator and will depend on ServiceLoader iteration order. This is a concrete ambiguity/behavior-change concern grounded in the diff, though whether selecting either provider is actually incorrect can’t be proven from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Most CryptoProvider methods (getAlgorithmProvider, getPemUtils, getCertificateUtils, getX509CertFactory, getSignature, getKeyPairGen, createECParams, etc.) throw UnsupportedOperationException while the provider is registered as the highest-availability service for the authz-client classloader. Any authz-client code path that grows to touch one of these methods (e.g., PEM parsing of a realm public key during token validation) crashes with a raw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime instead of a meaningful error about the missing capability.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new service-registered `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (META-INF/services entry) and forces crypto initialization in `AuthzClient.create(...)` via `CryptoIntegration.init(...)`. That provider implements `CryptoProvider` but most methods explicitly `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")` (e.g., `getPemUtils`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getX509CertFactory`, `getSignature`, `getKeyPairGen`, etc.). While the diff does not show any authz-client code path currently calling those unsupported methods (so a crash is not directly verifiable as introduced here), registering an incomplete `CryptoProvider` for the authz-client classloader does create a concrete, diff-grounded risk of raw runtime `UnsupportedOperationException` if any existing or future authz-client usage relies on those capabilities. The finding’s claim that it is the "highest-availability" provider isn’t strictly provable from the diff because other providers now have higher `order()` (200 vs 100), though they may not be present in the authz-client classpath.
